preamble: Deaffrication of the voiced postalveolar affricate /dʒ/ to the fricative /ʒ/. It happened in Late Old French (c. 1250–1300, along with tʃ > ʃ and ts > s), in Portuguese (Galician-Portuguese junio [ˈdʒuɲo] > junho [ˈʒuɲu]) and in urban Levantine Arabic, where ج is [ʒ] against Modern Standard Arabic [dʒ].

examples.note: /dʒ/ became /ʒ/ everywhere by Late Old French (c. 1250–1300).
Old Portuguese /dʒ/ (spelled j, and g before e/i) became /ʒ/.
Urban and female Levantine speech pronounces ج as /ʒ/; rural and male speech often keeps /dʒ/.
